title: Why Cities Pay for Michelin's Free 1900 Guide?｜Curio Archive
description:
Why did Michelin's free 1900 red booklet for drivers turn into a dining guide that tourism boards around the world pay to bring in?
For anyone who checks Michelin lists and wonders who really foots the bill—and whether stars can be bought.

From Clermont-Ferrand in 1889 to 35,000 free copies in 1900, the 7-franc relaunch without ads in 1920, anonymous inspectors, and stars—through tourism board deals in South Korea, Thailand, California, Colorado, and Taiwan, plus Tainan's four-year wait for its first star in 2026 and the two separate ledgers behind every guide.

Not affiliated with Michelin; sources verified through 2026-10-31 (including July 2026 Taiwan ceremony reports). AI-generated illustrations.

t001.text: The Michelin Guide awards one to three stars—yet in 1900, a French tire maker gave it away free!

t002.text: Rumors say stars are bought, yet tourism boards openly pay to bring the guide to town!

t003.text: At Taiwan's July 2026 Michelin ceremony honoring 61 starred spots, the Transport Minister spoke—

t004.text: Per Tourism data, the agency under him partnered to bring it in!

t005.text: Back in 2017, public funding for Seoul's guide sparked a parliamentary grilling over the fee;

t006.text: Foreign reports noted U.S. cities never paid—yet within years, America caved too!

t007.text: Today let's ask: how did a free booklet get cities paying a century later?

t008.text: Rewind to 1889 in Clermont-Ferrand, central France, where the Michelin brothers made tires.

t009.text: Today roads are packed; back then cars were brand-new and roads stood empty.

t011.text: Their plan: get people driving further.

t012.text: Drive further, wear tires faster, and come back for new ones.

t013.text: So in 1900, they printed 35,000 copies of the first guide—all free.

t014.text: Maps, tire-changing tips, fuel stops, plus places to eat and sleep.

t015.text: Yet stats cited by French auto press and Global Views show France had just 2,897 cars;

t016.text: If accurate, that's twelve copies stuffed in every car!

t018.text: A centennial biographer noted zero proof the free guide boosted tire sales.

t019.text: Across 126 years, three payers funded this book—first, Michelin's own tire business.

t020.text: Unsent free copies piled up in garages across France;

t021.text: Twenty years in, one sight killed the free giveaway forever—what did the founder see?

t022.text: Per Michelin's favorite official tale, in 1920 co-founder Andre Michelin entered a tire shop,

t023.text: and saw his beloved guides propping up a wobbly workbench!

t024.text: His verdict: people only truly respect what they pay for.

t025.text: Honestly, that line still sells memberships today.

t026.text: That same year, 1920, a new edition cost seven francs—making readers payer number two.

t027.text: It also stripped out all paid ads from the free era to block outside influence.

t028.text: To keep readers buying yearly, it needed a trump card—what arrived six years later?

t029.text: A single star: in 1926 the guide first starred fine restaurants—turning 100 this year!

t030.text: Five years later came the one-to-three-star system, with criteria published in 1936.

t031.text: One star means fine dining, two a detour, three a special trip;

t032.text: To me, that measures driving distance!

t033.text: Wait: if stars make or break restaurants, why trust inspectors aren't bribed?

t034.text: Beyond no ads, Michelin says mystery inspectors are full-time staff with zero outside ties,

t035.text: visiting anonymously many times and paying every bill.

t036.text: CommonWealth wrote one inspector dines at 250 spots a year.

t037.text: Flights, hotels, and meals—who can afford that global bill?

t038.text: Per US food outlet Eater citing the Financial Times, the guide lost over $24 million in 2011!

t039.text: Even with parent tire sales topping 20 billion euros in 2011, the guide couldn't bleed forever.

t040.text: Print sales fell short, so payer number three stepped up—tourism boards chasing global travelers!

t041.text: From 2016 came Singapore, Shanghai, Seoul, Taipei, and Bangkok;

t042.text: In 2017 via Eater, a former Michelin executive told the Washington Post governments sponsor guides.

t043.text: Key question: in US dollars, what does a Michelin contract cost?

t044.text: That October, Korea Times reported MP Song Ki-seok grilling officials over Seoul's deal:

t045.text: Per Song, Korea's tourism board owed Michelin 2 billion won—$1.8 million—through 2020; officials stayed mum.

t046.text: Note: it was accused of taking pay to publish in Korea, not selling stars;

t047.text: Yet Song questioned checks too: an Italian spot closed three months before print still made the cut!

t048.text: Michelin said the owner never told them in time.

t049.text: Amid the funding uproar, that Korea Times piece aired a chef's star-buying claim:

t050.text: She said a consultant pitched star help; she quit, and Michelin denied any link.

t051.text: I thought it was rumor—until two years later it hit broadcaster KBS!

t052.text: Korean press cited KBS saying spots won stars after fees; another chef sued over a 50-million-won demand.

t053.text: Michelin denied it, citing zero internal proof; no public ruling surfaced.

t054.text: Remember that Eater-cited line that US cities never paid? Did it hold up?

t055.text: From that report, it lasted just two years!

t056.text: In 2019 Visit California confirmed paying $600,000 to expand ratings beyond the Bay Area.

t057.text: Did early Asian backers regret it? In Feb 2017 Thailand's cabinet backed a five-year tourism plan,

t058.text: approving 143.5 million baht—not all for Michelin, yet did they stop before it expired?

t059.text: No—in late 2021 Thai tourism renewed for five more years!

t060.text: Its release claimed foreign dining spend doubled in 2019—the sponsor's own scorecard.

t061.text: After Asia renewed, more US cities joined: in 2023 Atlanta signed a three-year, $1 million deal;

t062.text: A Colorado paper checked: do our cities pay?

t063.text: Yes: from 2023, 70 to 100 thousand USD yearly.

t064.text: Yet the paper was clear: cash buys zero stars, only inspector visits.

t065.text: A Boston Globe column quipped that towns not paying get shut out.

t066.text: In October 2025 Michelin said ratings cost plenty and partners share travel;

t068.text: Taiwan chased it too: Global Views wrote tourism officials lobbied eight years for the March 2018 debut.

t069.text: PTS reported officials spent tens of millions of NT dollars on debut inspector evaluation costs;

t070.text: Yet CommonWealth wrote the prior year Michelin paid all fees—the two clash;

t071.text: Officials didn't explain rumored sums back then, so Taiwan's true total remains unfound.

t072.text: Still, official moves spoke clearly: in August 2024 the Minister said Michelin agreed to add two regions.

t073.text: Savor that word 'agreed'—who's waiting for whose nod?

t074.text: In 2025 New Taipei, Hsinchu County, and Hsinchu City joined—hailed as a ten-year plan milestone.

t075.text: Now that opening stage clicks: a tire maker's guide joined a ten-year state KPI, so the Minister spoke!

t076.text: Real test: when officials pay for visits, do stars rain down?

t077.text: Take July's gala: seven regions, 61 starred spots,

t078.text: yet stars hit just five—New Taipei and Hsinchu City got zero!

t079.text: Tainan joined in 2022, zero stars for years;

t080.text: Four years on in 2026, one star—open under a year!

t081.text: If public cash bought stars, why such split results?

t082.text: Scoring is private, yet calling tourism funds star-buying fails.

t083.text: If not star-buying, why pay for a once-free booklet?

t084.text: Recall its ad-free, self-paid pitch? Readers trust stars, so cities pay.

t085.text: Open those deals and there are two separate ledgers: one funds travel and city promotion;

t087.text: Michelin says deals don't sway stars; no court ruled any bought.

t088.text: Looking back—from the official workbench tale to the Minister's podium,

t089.text: three kinds of payers funded 126 years; only whether you trust that star stays unchanged.

t090.text: Case closed! Starred spot: line up or skip it?

t091.text: Comment below, and subscribe for more!
